The Asian Cup, initially scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia in early 2027, has been postponed until December next year following recent attacks on the kingdom, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said on Tuesday. A strike on Riyadh's international airport last month killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement claiming responsibility for the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The tournament's organising committee said the tournament had been rescheduled "in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions."

item.content:encoded:
GLOBAL MARKETS-Asian stocks retreat ahead of US midterms, oil steadies Reuters | Updated: 03-11-2026 11:33 IST | Created: 03-11-2026 11:33 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Asian tech stocks came under fresh pressure on Tuesday as investors fretted over AI spending and earnings, while oil prices stabilised after the previous session's tumble ahead of the start of voting for the US midterm elections. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 1.4% at the lowest level since October 23, led by a decline of as much as 4.1% in South Korean shares. European futures fell 0.9%, German DAX futures slid 0.8% and FTSE futures were 0.2% lower. Taiwanese shares slid 3.3%, putting the local benchmark on track to confirm a technical correction after extending losses to 13.1% from a record high in early October. Shares in China fell 1.4%, with investors disappointed at the latest moves by authorities to shore up a market that is the year's weakest performer among major indexes. S&P 500 e-mini futures edged lower for a fourth consecutive day, off 0.1%, while Japanese markets were closed for a holiday. "Within Asia, Korea and Taiwan equity outflows continue to dominate, given rising concerns around sustainability of the tech cycle," Bank of America analysts wrote in a note. Australian shares bucked the trend, rising 0.3%, and the Aussie dollar slipped 0.3% to $0.6978 after the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted its cash rate target, as expected, but with a 6-3 split vote and hints it might be on hold for a while. Overnight, stocks on Wall Street edged lower, with the S&P 500 slipping 0.5%. Apple shares extended losses, falling 2.8% in after-hours trading after the iPhone maker on Monday forecast lower gross margins for the crucial holiday quarter, citing rising memory-chip costs, and projected services revenue growth that fell well short of Wall Street expectations. MIDTERM ELECTIONS Investors are also preparing for voting in the US midterm elections, where President Donald Trump's Republican Party is facing a challenge to keep its hold on Congress. "Tuesday will be nothing more than the day ahead of a much bigger day," ING analysts wrote in a note. By tomorrow, the market will have guidance on the midterm implications and the US Treasury's quarterly refunding announcement, they wrote. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was up 2.1 basis points at 4.913%. Opinion polls favour the Democrats to win the House, though the Senate remains too close to call. Prediction market sites Polymarket and Kalshi currently assign probabilities of 77% and 76%, respectively, that the Democrats will control the Senate. A surprise Republican sweep would likely lift yields and the dollar, said Steve Englander, co-head of FX research at Standard Chartered. Investors are watching the race for Texas governor because the Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa is proposing a moratorium on data centre building, said Brent Donnelly, president at FX analytics firm Spectra Markets. Oil prices steadied after a fall, with Brent crude up 0.5% at $105.30 in Asian trading as investors weighed the state of peace talks between the US and Iran. The US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, a US official told Reuters on Monday, confirming an earlier Wall Street Journal report. Against the Chinese yuan, the US dollar was 0.4% stronger at 6.6720 yuan after the People’s Bank of China said it would raise the foreign exchange reserve ratio, a move aimed at putting the brakes on a long rally in the yuan. Cryptocurrencies remained choppy after last week's Binance hack, as customers withdrew a net $4.72 billion of funds. Bitcoin nudged 0.1% higher to $76,822.21 and ether declined 0.2% to $2,250.41.

item.content:encoded:
WRAPUP 1-Trump faces midterm verdict with control of Congress at stake Reuters | Updated: 03-11-2026 11:32 IST | Created: 03-11-2026 11:32 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

American voters will deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump's second term in Tuesday's midterm elections, with polls and nonpartisan analysts favoring Democrats to wrest the House from Republicans while control of the Senate remains uncertain. The battle for the Senate is unfolding across nearly 10 closely contested statewide races, most in Republican strongholds. History is against Trump's Republicans: the sitting president's party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterm elections since World War Two. Trump's approval rating is hovering near his all-time lows, dragged down by deep voter frustration over the war with Iran and the resulting rise in fuel prices. There is little doubt this year's election is all about Trump, the central US political figure for most of the last decade. Trump himself has told his supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot," a message Democratic leaders have happily echoed. The president has sought to energize his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, the vast majority in states he easily won in 2024, underscoring the extent to which Republicans are playing defense. Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history," Trump said on Monday during a speech in Washington. But opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump's handling of the issue, after his sweeping tariff policy and his decision to attack Iran in February increased domestic costs. Republican candidates, meanwhile, have struggled to distance themselves from a president who demands fealty and rarely acknowledges mistakes. All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election, along with 35 of the Senate's 100 seats, though the majority of contests are not considered competitive. Democrats must flip at least three House seats and four Senate seats to win a majority in each chamber. A Democratic House or Senate could launch investigations into what Democrats describe as self-dealing by the Trump administration and demand concessions to approve legislation. A Democratic Senate would also have the power to block Trump appointments, including US Supreme Court nominations if vacancies arise. But while Democrats have put Republicans on the defensive on much of their home turf, they have little margin for error. The party must defend all of its current seats, including a tight race in Michigan, while winning at least two states that voted for Trump by a double-digit margin two years ago: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Opinion polls show Democrats either narrowly leading or within striking distance in all of those states. MICHIGAN RACE ROILED BY CROSS-PARTY ENDORSEMENT The Michigan Senate contest between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, 42, and Republican former US Representative Mike Rogers, 63, received a fresh jolt on Sunday, when Democrat Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the party's primary election, endorsed Rogers in a surprise reversal. In addition to the implications for Senate control, the Michigan race represents a high-profile test of whether Republicans' identity-based attacks – El-Sayed would be the nation's first Muslim senator — prove effective in a battleground state. A win for El-Sayed, who has criticized Israel and supports liberal policies such as universal healthcare, would also be seen as a boost for the party's left wing ahead of the 2028 presidential election. The Alaska Senate race has been caught up in its own turmoil, after the New York Times reported that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, 53, helped recruit a third candidate who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, 61. Peltola has denied involvement. Trump's Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations and filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election results, though a judge dismissed the latter effort. In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, 37, has his party once again dreaming of winning the biggest Republican state after decades of heartbreak. His scandal-plagued opponent, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, 63, has benefited from a nine-figure investment from the world's richest man, Elon Musk, who has spent hundreds of millions of dollars boosting Republicans. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton, 62, a megachurch pastor, held a narrow polling lead over Republican US Senator Roger Marshall, 66. The state voted for Trump by more than 16 percentage points in 2024 and has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. And in Maine, Republican US Senator Susan Collins, 73, is once again seeking to defy the Democratic leanings of her home state and win a sixth term. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, 58, a former state senate president who unexpectedly became the nominee after Democratic oyster farmer Graham Platner dropped out amid accusations of misconduct, which he denied. Other competitive Senate races are taking place in Iowa, Nebraska, Ohio and South Carolina, all Republican-held seats. TRUMP'S JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INTERVENES There are 47 US House races widely seen as competitive, according to a Reuters analysis of the leading election forecasters. If the other contests all proceed as predicted, Democrats would need to win only 13 of those 46 races to secure a majority. The fight for the House has been waged largely on Republican turf, including some districts Trump carried by double digits in 2024. A Trump-backed Republican effort to redraw districts in several states to make them safer for the party appears not to have yielded the gains the White House expected. Democrats have warned that Trump, who has long falsely claimed that US elections are rigged, may attempt to challenge Tuesday's results if Republicans lose. In addition to its actions in Alaska, Trump's Justice Department also filed a lawsuit in California to block ballots it says may be invalid, a break from decades of practice meant to insulate elections from political influence. The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday rejected the administration's request for an emergency order in the case. Three dozen governors' races will also take place on Tuesday, as well as thousands of state-level legislative contests and ballot measures on everything from a billionaires' tax to abortion rights.

item.description: Actor John Goodman has opened up about the physical and emotional adjustments following his 200-pound weight loss, admitting that he is still getting used to his changed appearance and that the ...
item.content:encoded:
"My body's too messed up": John Goodman opens up about adjusting to life after 200-pound weight loss Actor John Goodman has opened up about the physical and emotional adjustments following his 200-pound weight loss, admitting that he is still getting used to his changed appearance and that the transformation has left his body with some lasting effects, according to E! News. ANI | Updated: 03-11-2026 10:03 IST | Created: 03-11-2026 10:03 IST

John Goodman (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Actor John Goodman has opened up about the physical and emotional adjustments following his 200-pound weight loss, admitting that he is still getting used to his changed appearance and that the transformation has left his body with some lasting effects, according to E! News. The 74-year-old actor, known for 'Roseanne' and 'The Righteous Gemstones', revealed that he even turned down a nude scene in the HBO comedy 'The Righteous Gemstones' because he was uncomfortable with how his body might look on camera after losing so much weight. Speaking on the November 2 episode of the 'Happy Sad Confused' podcast, Goodman recalled how he initially expressed concerns about appearing nude in the series, which ran for four seasons from 2019 to 2025. "I thought I was going to have to be naked in it and I said, 'I don't know. My body's too messed up losing all this weight,'" he said, adding that he and the crew eventually worked out a way to complete the scene, as per the outlet. The actor also spoke about adjusting to his new appearance, saying that even his face sometimes looks unfamiliar to him. "I'm still trying to get used to my face," he said. "It's weird. I think of myself as one way and then I look at myself, 'Oh, wow!'" "It's strange. It's fun to get used to. There's a lot of stuff I'm getting used to," he added. Reflecting on his life before the transformation, Goodman wondered whether his struggles with weight had affected his professional journey, describing his past behaviour as a possible form of "self-sabotage". "I was working enough as I was," he said. "I wasn't crazy about it, but I wonder if I probably sabotaged myself." Goodman has previously spoken candidly about his long struggle with weight. In an interview with The New Yorker published on October 18, the actor recalled how his eating habits remained unhealthy even after he stopped drinking alcohol in 2007. He described himself as "eating alcoholically" during that period and said his weight had reached "almost 400 pounds" at its highest. "I'd lose 60 pounds in a summer, gain it all back. 70 pounds, 80 pounds," Goodman recalled, adding that the repeated cycle of losing and regaining weight eventually became exhausting. The actor eventually lost around 200 pounds after undergoing stomach surgery. However, he said the transformation also brought some physical challenges, including anaemia and increased sensitivity to cold. "I also turned anemic and lost a layer of fat under my skin, and I'm cold all the time," he said, according to E! News. Goodman, who is married to Anna Beth Goodman, is now focusing on improving his physical strength, balance and overall fitness as he adjusts to the changes. "Basically, building up the core, balance, strength training, stuff like that, so I don't fall down," he said. He also recalled suffering a fall shortly after returning to London following a Christmas break, which resulted in a fractured hip. "I came down parallel to the ground, on my hip, and fractured it," he said, as per the outlet. The actor is now concentrating on building strength and maintaining his health as he continues to adapt to life following his dramatic weight-loss transformation. (ANI)
